test_title: PYST 41: RRB Group D - GS (Held On: 15 Dec, 2025 Shift 2)
subject: general
question: In human beings, how is the sex of a child determined?

options.text: By the difference in number of chromosomes inherited by the child
By the inheritance of X or Y chromosome from the father
By the environmental conditions prevailing during development of the foetus
By the inheritance of an X chromosome from the mother

solution:
The correct answer is __**By the inheritance of X or Y chromosome from the father**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In human beings, every cell contains **23 pairs** of chromosomes, making a total of **46** chromosomes. Out of these, **22 pairs** are called **autosomes** and are identical in both males and females.
 
• The **23rd pair** of chromosomes is known as the **sex chromosome**, which differs between the two sexes. Females possess two **X chromosomes (XX)**, while males possess one **X** and one **Y chromosome (XY)**.
 
• During the process of **gametogenesis**, the mother produces **eggs (ova)** that always carry a single **X chromosome**. Therefore, the maternal contribution to the child's sex is always the same.
 
• The **father** produces two types of **sperm**: approximately **50%** carry an **X chromosome** and the other **50%** carry a **Y chromosome**.
 
• The sex of the child is determined at the moment of **fertilization**. If a sperm carrying an **X chromosome** fertilizes the egg, the resulting **zygote** will be **XX**, developing into a **female**. If a sperm carrying a **Y chromosome** fertilizes the egg, the **zygote** will be **XY**, developing into a **male**. ***Hence, statement 2 is the correct mechanism.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Heterogametic Sex:** In humans, the **male** is the **heterogametic sex** because he produces two different types of gametes (X and Y), whereas the female is **homogametic** as she produces only one type (X).
 
• **The SRY Gene:** The **Sex-determining Region Y (SRY)** gene, located on the **Y chromosome**, is the master switch that triggers the development of male physical characteristics. In the absence of this gene, the embryo develops into a female.
 
• **Probability of Sex:** Statistically, there is a **50:50 chance** of having a boy or a girl in each pregnancy, as the segregation of **X** and **Y** chromosomes into sperm occurs randomly during **meiosis**.
 
• **Genetic vs. Environmental Determination:** Unlike some reptiles (such as **crocodiles** and **turtles**) where the **incubation temperature** of the eggs determines the sex, human sex determination is strictly **genetic** and is not influenced by **environmental conditions** during the development of the **foetus**.
 
• **Chromosomal Abnormalities:** Sometimes, errors in cell division can lead to variations in the **23rd pair**, such as **Turner syndrome (XO)** or **Klinefelter syndrome (XXY)**, which affect physical and reproductive development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Mendelian Inheritance:** The inheritance of sex follows **Mendel’s laws** of segregation, where alleles (in this case, sex chromosomes) separate during gamete formation.
 
• **Historical Context:** The discovery of the **XY sex-determination system** was made by **Nettie Stevens** and **Edmund Beecher Wilson** independently in **1905**.
 
• **Misconceptions:** It is a common biological fact that the **mother** does not determine the sex of the child; however, in many cultures, women have been historically blamed for not giving birth to a male child despite the **biological determination** coming from the **paternal sperm**.
